tip: When a phrase like 'unter keinen Umständen' opens the sentence, the verb still comes second, so the subject follows it: 'dürfen Sie'.
'Einen Cappuccino' takes the masculine accusative ending -en on 'ein'; neuter 'ein Croissant' stays plain 'ein'.
The passive is 'wird' + past participle: 'wird ... gebacken' = is baked. Here 'wird' is not future tense.
After 'das', an adjective before the noun takes the ending -e: 'das schwierige Examen'.
After 'ist' the adjective takes no ending: 'alt' stays bare. Before a noun it would decline: 'das alte Auto'.
'Trotz' (despite) takes the genitive: 'trotz der Müdigkeit'.
'Mit' always takes the dative, and the dative plural adds -n: 'mit den Dokumenten'.
A superlative before a noun uses 'der/die/das' plus -ste: 'das älteste Gebäude' = the oldest building.
The stray 'vor' at the end belongs to 'vorlesen' (read aloud): it splits off from 'lese' and parks at the clause end. Without it, 'lesen' just means read.
As the direct object, 'er' (he/it) becomes 'ihn' (him/it): 'er repariert ihn'.
'Man' is the generic subject 'one' or 'people in general' and uses the 'er/sie/es' verb form: 'sollte man'.
With no article, the adjective carries the gender signal itself: 'frisches Obst' uses the -es ending to flag that 'Obst' is a 'das' word.
'Guter Rat ist teuer' is a set proverb, said when you are stuck and a good solution is hard to find; literally, good advice is expensive.
'Brille' is singular in German, even though English 'glasses' is plural: 'eine neue Brille' = one pair of glasses.
German waits on, not for: 'warten auf', so 'wartet auf seine Mutter' is literally waits on his mother where English says waits for.
Plural 'die' forces the -en ending on the adjective: 'die kleinen Kinder'. It stays -en for every adjective after a plural 'die'.
After 'ein' (neuter), the adjective takes -es: 'ein interessantes Buch'. The -es carries the neuter marker the article leaves off.
'Leihen' marks the person receiving in the dative: 'seinem Mitbewohner' = to his roommate.
'Kennenlernen' is separable, so 'zu' goes inside it: 'kennenzulernen', not 'zu kennenlernen'.
To negate a noun, use 'kein', which declines like 'ein': 'keinen Parkplatz' = not any parking space (masculine accusative).
'Musst ... nicht' means 'don't have to', not 'must not'. For a ban you would say 'darfst nicht'.
'Kein ... mehr' means 'not any more': 'keine Lust mehr' = doesn't feel like it anymore.
'Vertrauen' takes a dative object, not accusative: 'sie vertraut dem erfahrenen Bergführer' = she trusts the experienced guide.
Verbs ending in -ieren form the participle without ge-: 'funktioniert', not 'gefunktioniert'.
After 'die' (singular feminine), the adjective takes -e: 'die neue Lehrerin'.
Inseparable prefixes like ver- drop the ge- in the participle: 'verdoppelt', not 'geverdoppelt'.
'An' + 'dem' contracts to 'am' for days and weekends: 'am Wochenende' = on the weekend.
Add -erweise to an adjective to comment on the whole sentence: 'bedauerlicherweise' = regrettably.
German normally adds 'gern' to a verb instead of using a 'to like' verb: 'nicht gern' = doesn't like doing it.
'Nachbar' belongs to a small group of nouns that add -n whenever they are not the subject: 'dem Nachbarn'.
